_README: UNTRIAGED. Every key here was surfaced on 2026-09-04 by widening this lint's walk to the whole server AND teaching it the inline route-handler shape. Until that day the route layer was not merely unscanned but UNSCANNABLE: a route file's units are anonymous `async (req, res) => {}` callbacks, which neither extractor could see, so every query in every handler was attributed to the enclosing registerRoutes() — a 1,400-line unit that mentions organizationId, so rule 1 could never fire on any of them. Adding extractRouteHandlers took the visible unit count from 0 route handlers to 2,668 and the offender count from 57 to 217.
_WHY_A_SEPARATE_FILE: These are NOT the same kind of entry as the registers inside check-org-scoped-fetch.mjs. Each of those was read by a human and carries a recorded reason. These 210 were not. Mixing them would quietly convert 'verified safe' into 'has been seen by a regex', which is the exact dishonesty this repository's gates exist to prevent. They live apart so the distinction survives, and so the burn-down is countable.
_THE_OBLIGATION: This file may only SHRINK. It is a debt register, not an exemption list, and only the 8 keys listed under _TRIAGED have been read. A debt register whose entries nobody has opened is not a smaller problem than an unscanned directory; it is the same problem with a number attached. Triage moves an entry either into a real fix or into the hand-verified register inside check-org-scoped-fetch.mjs with a written reason. A sample of ~57 of these was triaged before this landed and produced two REAL cross-tenant defects out of the sample (routes-doc-system.ts's seller/buyer reads and POST /api/investor-profiles' tenant-assignment injection, both fixed in 779bc251), so the expectation is that more remain in here.
_WHAT_IT_DOES_NOT_EXCUSE: A NEW offender is not covered by this file and fails the gate immediately. That is the point of landing the widening now rather than after the burn-down: eight live cross-tenant paths were found by hand in files this lint had never opened, and every day it stayed blind was another day a ninth could be written without anything noticing.
_POPULATION_CORRECTION_2026_09_04: These 8 entries were added the same day the register was created, and they are
the ONLY entries in it that carry an individual reason — because they are the
only ones that have been read.
The route extractor originally took 'the LAST `async (` inside the registration
call' as the handler. The call text spans the handler's whole body, so a nested
`db.transaction(async (tx) => ...)` is later in the string than the handler
itself and won: 51 of 2620 handlers were read at the wrong boundary. It also
dropped every handler written with a TRAILING COMMA before the closing paren
(432 of them) and every handler registered through a wrapper such as
`asyncHandler(...)` (40). Fixing the boundary raised the readable population
from 2142 to 2668 handlers and query chains from 1831 to 2040, and these 8
findings are what had been hiding behind it.
Each was read before being written down. None is a live cross-tenant read; the
reasons are in _TRIAGED. The other 210 keys have NOT been read — that is the
difference between this block and the rest of the file, and the obligation
above is to close that gap, not to copy this note onto them.
Nine further entries were REMOVED the same day, not added: each was a query
inside a route handler that had ALSO been attributed to the file's enclosing
registrar (registerRoutes, registerMiscRoutes), so every finding in a route
file was being reported twice — once against a handler you can act on, and
once against a 1,400-line function whose name tells a reader nothing. Queries
are now attributed to their INNERMOST unit; a query written directly in a
registrar body, outside every handler, still belongs to it and is still read.
